title: Banku
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Two cups of cornmeal soured until the dough begins to bubble, then stirred into boiling salted water for about fifteen minutes with a spoon strong enough not to break.
longDesc: Banku is the smooth, sour, stretchy swallow eaten with okra stew and grilled tilapia, and unlike kenkey it is cooked all the way through rather than half-cooked and recombined. Two cups of white stone-ground cornmeal and two teaspoons of corn starch are mixed with two cups of lukewarm water and left in a warm place for several days, stirred once a day — and this recipe, unlike the same author's kenkey, gives a real cue: the dough should begin to bubble up as it ferments. The dough is then stirred gradually into two cups of boiling salted water for about fifteen minutes.
ingredients: 2 cups white stone-ground cornmeal — not masa harina
Extra water, as needed to prevent scorching
equipment: Strong wooden spoon or paddle — something flimsy will likely break
steps: Mix the cornmeal and corn starch with the 2 cups of lukewarm water.
Cover lightly and leave to sit in a warm place — counter, stove top or oven — for several days, stirring once a day.
The dough should begin to bubble up as it ferments.
// ENDPOINT: bubbling, plus sourness to taste. For a first attempt, about 2 days will be long enough; the more days, the more sour.
If you stirred the dough every day it should not have mould on it, but if there is any, scrape it off before using.
Boil the 2 cups of water with the salt in a 3-quart saucepan.
Gradually stir in the fermented dough.
Stir for about 15 minutes with a strong wooden spoon or paddle, adding water as needed to prevent scorching.
Cool slightly, wet your hands, and shape into one large or several small loaves.
chefTips: The bubbling cue is what makes banku publishable where this author's kenkey recipe is not — the dough visibly rises and bubbles as it ferments, and that is an endpoint you can see.
Two days for a first attempt, her own advice. Longer is more sour, and you can always go further next time.
A strong wooden spoon, and she means it: something flimsy will likely break. Fifteen minutes of stirring a stiffening corn dough is genuinely hard work.
Stir the dough in gradually. All at once and it lumps instantly.
Add water as needed to prevent scorching rather than to thin it. Banku should be stiff.
Stir daily during the ferment and there usually will be no mould. If there is, scrape it off before the dough goes near the pot.

A traditional-producer study of banku in Côte d'Ivoire gives the best sensory description anywhere: properly fermented, it should smell slightly sour but not unpleasant, like a rising bread dough. Over-fermented does not taste good.
commonMistakes: Adding the dough to the water all at once.
Thinning it with too much water.
Fermenting far past the bubbling stage on a first attempt.
sources: QUANTITIES AND METHOD adapted from two consecutive posts by the same author. 'Recipe #7: Banku, 4 choices', betumiblog.blogspot.com, Thursday 13 August 2009, byline as printed 'Posted by Fran at 3:50 PM'; and 'Recipe #7, continued (banku)', Monday 17 August 2009, byline 'Posted by Fran at 3:45 PM'. Quantities TWO-PASS.
Opening of the first post, verbatim: 'Yesterday I mentioned I'd begun fermenting some cornmeal to make the dough for the Ghanaian dish known as banku.'
Ingredients exactly as printed: '2 cups of white Indian Head cornmeal (or other similar stone ground cornmeal, but do not use masa harina)'; '2 teaspoons of corn starch'; '2 cups of lukewarm water'.

THE FERMENTATION INSTRUCTION AND ITS CUE, verbatim and TWO-PASS: 'cover lightly and leave to sit in a warm place (counter, stove top or oven) for several days, stirring once a day'. And then the cue this recipe has and her kenkey recipe does not: 'The dough should begin to bubble up as it ferments.' The printed duration is 'several days'. The second post adds, verbatim: 'the more days you let the dough ferment, the more sour it will be. If it's your first time, probably 2 days will be long enough.' And: 'If you stirred the dough every day it should not have mold on it, but if there is any, scrap it off before adding the dough to the boiling water.' — 'scrap' as printed.

COOKING METHOD, TWO-PASS: boil 2 cups water with 1 teaspoon salt in a 3-quart saucepan and 'gradually stir in the fermented dough'; stir for 'about 15 minutes using a strong wooden spoon or paddle (something flimsy will likely break)'; add water as needed to prevent scorching; cool slightly, wet hands and shape. 'Banku is usually eaten warm or lukewarm.' YIELD: no count is printed; the shaping instruction is 'shape the banku into one large or several small loaves'.

WITHIN-AUTHOR DISAGREEMENT across her three fermented posts, recorded and not averaged: banku 'several days' with a bubbling cue and 'probably 2 days' for a first time; kenkey about 3 days with only a relative sourness cue (GHA037); akple described as made from UNFERMENTED corn dough (GHA042).

THE BEST SENSORY DESCRIPTION OF BANKU FERMENTATION IS IVORIAN, NOT GHANAIAN, and is labelled as such: Krabi E.A.R., Bouatenin K.M.J.-P., Kouamé K.A., Fofana I.F., Koussemon M., 'Microbiological and nutritional quality of banku a fermented maize and cassava-based food consumed in West Africa', Romanian Biotechnology Letters 28(4):4040-4048, 2023, sampling five female producers each in Grand-Bassam and Gonzagueville in traditional settings. CUE, TWO-PASS and confirmed present in the text: 'When properly fermented, it should have a slightly sour, but not unpleasant aroma, "like a rising bread dough." An over-fermented mixture does not taste good.' Its process, TWO-PASS: '3 to 4 volumes of corn paste are mixed with 1 volume of cassava paste'; 'The mixture is mixed well by hand and the container is covered with a clean cloth for a three-day fermentation in a warm place at 37°C or in the upper part of the refrigerator.' Its pH and titratable acidity: fermented maize flour pH 4.18 ± 0.52 and TA 0.31 ± 0.01%; fermented cassava dough pH 3.58 ± 0.04, TA 0.27 ± 0.04; the mixture pH 3.53 ± 0.04, TA 0.18 ± 0.01; final cooked banku pH 4.07 ± 0.08, TA 0.05 ± 0.01.

NO GHANAIAN BANKU FERMENTATION STUDY WITH pH WAS FOUND, and that is a real gap. Ghanaian theses mention banku only in passing. The FAO bulletin 'Fermented cereals: a global perspective' gives banku as 'steeping 24 hrs followed by wet milling and fermentation for 3 days' with 'lactic acid bacteria and moulds', and a ratio of '4 parts dough to 2 parts water' — but THAT RATIO IS THE DOUGH-TO-WATER RATIO FOR COOKING, NOT a maize-to-cassava ratio, and it is recorded here so it is not misread as one.

A NOTE ON COMPOSITION, unreconciled: this recipe uses CORNMEAL ONLY, with corn starch. The Ivorian study and the FAO bulletin both describe banku as a corn AND CASSAVA dough. Her own akple post (GHA042) is labelled 'banku' among its tags and does combine corn and cassava dough. So whether banku requires cassava is not settled by these sources, and the corn-only version is published as printed.

HER OTHER THREE 'CHOICES' from the first post, recorded: commercial Nina International products — a dried powder of corn and cassava, frozen corn-and-cassava dough, and frozen corn-only dough. She prefers the frozen; the powder 'has an aftertaste'.

A POINT SHE CITES FROM A NAMED SCIENTIST, Professor Sefa-Dedeh: 'the actual bacteria that grow during the fermentation process are specific to Ghana, and will also produce a different flavor to the dough.' That is the honest caveat on making banku outside Ghana.
RELATED, not banku: Amoa-Awua, Owusu, Feglo 2005 on agbelima from high-quality cassava flour reached pH 4.11-3.82 in 48 h. That is a lab cassava-flour system, not banku. SINGLE-PASS.
storage: 2 days refrigerated, wrapped. It firms up considerably.
reheating: Steam, or microwave wrapped in damp paper. Eaten warm or lukewarm.
healthBenefits: Fermentation reduces phytate and raises B-vitamin availability.
The acidity lowers the glycaemic response compared with unfermented maize.
culturalNote: Banku with grilled tilapia and a pot of shito is the Ghanaian meal most likely to be eaten at a plastic table by the roadside with a cold drink, and it is as close to a national dish as anything in the country. The fifteen minutes of hard stirring is why banku sellers have forearms like bricklayers.
